title: Rokib Al Dhin Raadh - When the Update Is Not a Gradient
description:
​Every standard convergence proof for gradient descent assumes that each update is a gradient. Self-repairing training violates that assumption by design, and it still converges. This session shows why, and exactly where the proof stops.

Zero out a converged convolutional layer at epoch 100. A parameter-matched baseline remains at chance on every seed (10.0% ± 0.0%). A self-repairing network recovers to 80.3% ± 1.6% through 85 bounded, logged corrections. Those corrections are state-dependent, diagnostic-triggered and discontinuous; they are the gradient of no objective. Why the trajectory does not diverge is a genuinely mathematical question.

We model training as a switched dynamical system (contractive gradient flow, bounded disturbance, isolated resets) and derive a practical input-to-state stability bound under local L-smoothness and α-strong convexity:

limsup ‖θₜ − θ*‖ ≤ γ = 2βM/α + ε_max/(ηα)

The bound is non-vacuous only if correction magnitude decays, so the stability claim becomes a falsifiable prediction. Within a 383-run evaluation, it holds: correction magnitude falls by 83–93%.

The most instructive part is the gap between theory and observation. The per-step contraction the proof relies on holds on only 31.6% of steps, yet the run converges. The offset term never vanishes, so the result is practical rather than strict ISS. Forward invariance of the neighbourhood remains unproven.

We close on the open problems: deriving ε(t) from first principles, relaxing strong convexity to Polyak–Łojasiewicz, and dwell-time conditions for discrete reinitializations. Attendees are invited to challenge the bound directly.
preprint: https://zenodo.org/records/21730363

​Bio:
Rokib Al Dhin Raadh is an 18y old researcher working on the stability and auditability of neural network training dynamics, without institutional affiliation. He is the sole author of ORMAS, an architecture that localizes, repairs and logs its own component-level failures during training, validated across 383 controlled experiments on four architectures. His input-to-state stability analysis of self-repairing training was accepted at DeepMath 2026 (Conference on the Mathematical Theory of Deep Neural Networks) after double-blind review. He serves as a reviewer for the NeurIPS 2026 Trustworthy AI for Good workshop and is a member of the Cohere Labs Open Science Community. He is the founder of Oxiedo.

title: AI Realism Workflow the Pros Use (Eleven v4 + Seedance 2.5)
description:
Keep your AI film characters sounding the same in every scene with Eleven v4 and Seedance 2.5.

Create AI Films → https://elevenlabs.io/creative?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=trend_tutorials&utm_content=create_consistent_character_voices_with_eleven_v4_and_seedance_2_5_ai_workflow

One of the biggest problems in AI filmmaking is characters losing their voice between scenes. In this workflow, we walk through how to pair Eleven v4 voice generation with Seedance 2.5 inside ElevenCreative so your character keeps the same voice, emotion, and delivery across every shot. We start by generating the perfect delivery in Eleven v4 using audio tags to direct the performance, then storyboard the scene in Flows with the voice over in place before generating any video.

From there we cover three ways to use that voice generation as a reference in Seedance 2.5, each one making the result more consistent:

• Method 1 • Use the Eleven v4 generation as an audio reference alongside a character reference and a set reference, then prompt the scene with tagged references
• Method 2 • Convert the MP3 into a plain black MP4 video and use it as a video reference, which tends to extract the delivery more reliably than the audio file
• Method 3 • Add a timestamp transcript from the black video using an LLM node, tag it in your prompt, and offset the timestamps so the action (like a crash landing) lands before the character starts speaking

We also cover choosing a voice from the Great voices for Eleven v4 selection in the voice library, lip syncing the generation to your character in Flows, and generating the scene separately so you can control the background. By the third method you can focus entirely on the prompt and the action while the voice delivery stays consistent every time.

title: Turning Stranded Energy Into Intelligence: Crusoe CEO Chase Lochmiller
description:
Chase Lochmiller runs one of the most operationally complex companies in AI: Crusoe builds power plants, manufactures electrical equipment, operates gigawatt-scale data centers, and runs a managed AI cloud on top, all under one roof. He just closed a round at a $31 billion valuation, and he got there by selling off the Bitcoin mining business that was paying the bills.

Chase explains why Crusoe is modeled on Exxon, not a cloud provider, and why he partners with companies that look like competitors. He makes the case that a company that outgrows the person who got it there is the rule, not the exception, and that CEOs almost always fire too slowly. He also talks candidly about hiring a coach, working hard to become a polished speaker when it didn’t come naturally, and why the data center industry’s biggest problem is a marketing problem.

I meet with a group of Sequoia founder CEOs between 20 and 2,000 employees, and one of them told me his business is becoming dizzyingly complex beneath him. Chase has the clearest answer I’ve heard for how to hold that in your head. 

And yes, we talk about summiting Everest.

title: Confronting Our AI Future: Closing Keynote "Discovery Loop" with Jeff Dean and Fei-Fei Li
description:
This closing fireside chat brings together two of the field's most consequential builders — Jeff Dean, whose work at Google has helped define the modern AI stack, and Fei-Fei Li, whose case for human-centered AI has shaped how the field thinks about who this technology should actually serve. Coming at the end of a day spent grappling with AI's risks and unresolved questions, the conversation turns to where the two of them agree, where they don't, and what they think the choices ahead really come down to.

*Speakers:* 

- Fei-Fei Li: Inaugural Sequoia Professor in the Computer Science Department at Stanford University, and a Founding Director of HAI. She served as the Director of Stanford’s AI Lab from 2013 to 2018. Li has served as a Vice President at Google and Chief Scientist of AI/ML at Google Cloud (2017-2018), board member or advisor in various public or private companies and is currently a Co-founder/CEO of World Labs, an AI company focusing on Spatial Intelligence and generative AI. 

- Jeff Dean: Computer scientist and software engineer. He is best known for his work at Google, which he joined in 1999. He led Google AI from 2018 to 2023 and was Google's chief scientist from 2023 to 2026. Dean co-founded the AI research start-up Discovery Loop in 2026.
